title: Sony and Warner Chappell sue Anthropic over lyrics, name Amodei and Mann personally
subtitle: The complaint alleges training on tens of thousands of songs — including 'I Am the Walrus' and 'Hallelujah' — sourced from Library Genesis and the Pirate Library Mirror, seeking up to $150,000 per work.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell Music filed suit against Anthropic in California federal court on August 29, alleging the company trained its Claude models on tens of thousands of copyrighted compositions without permission. The 48-page complaint identifies specific catalog works — 'I Am the Walrus' and Leonard Cohen's 'Hallelujah' among them — and traces the alleged training corpus to Library Genesis and the Pirate Library Mirror, two shadow-library archives long known in the copyright-litigation record. The publishers are seeking statutory damages of up to $150,000 per willfully infringed work, plus up to $25,000 for each removal of copyright management information. Anthropic co-founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann are named as personal defendants.

The mechanism the complaint attacks is the pipeline, not the output. Earlier music-publisher suits against Anthropic (Universal, Concord, and ABKCO in 2023; the January 2026 consolidated action covering 20,000-plus works) argued Claude reproduces lyrics on request. This new filing argues that acquisition of the training set itself — from repositories the plaintiffs say are demonstrably pirated — is the infringement, and that naming the founders reflects a claim they directed and personally benefited from that acquisition.

The context is a copyright docket already dense: Anthropic settled a book-authors class action for $1.5 billion in the summer, and 2026 has produced a steady drumbeat of publisher and rights-holder complaints across labs. What is new here is the combination — a named-founder theory, shadow-library sourcing as the core allegation, and two of the three biggest music publishers filing together. The remedy sought, at the high end, would exceed the book settlement.

Takeaway for learners: 'the AI copyright question' is not one question. Training data acquisition, model outputs, and the identity of the actor being sued are separate legal theories, and courts are answering them separately. If you are studying AI policy or considering AI work at any level of the stack, get comfortable reading the distinction between how a model learned something and what it says — because the next few years of case law will hinge on that line, and where the line ends up will decide what building any of this is allowed to look like.
